---
title: "Grids, hexagons, and a small game"
---

Bees pack their comb with hexagons because hexagons cover a surface with no gap
left over. Your loops can lay out the same pattern, and a bee can then walk from
cell to cell. Start with circles though, since a circle needs one radius
and a hexagon needs six corner points.

## Five circles, then twenty-five {#sec-beehive-rows}

1. Create a new app `packing-experiment` from our template inside
   `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace the `<h1>` line with this:

   ```html
   <h1>Packing experiment</h1>
   <svg id="board" viewBox="0 0 300 260" width="300" height="260" role="img" aria-label="Circles placed by a loop"></svg>
   ```

3. Replace both lines of `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';

   const board = document.querySelector<SVGSVGElement>('#board');
   if (!board) {
     throw new Error('The page has no board');
   }

   const STEP = 52;

   for (let col = 0; col < 5; col++) {
     const dot = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
     dot.setAttribute('cx', String(26 + col * STEP));
     dot.setAttribute('cy', '26');
     dot.setAttribute('r', '26');
     dot.setAttribute('fill', '#f7d774');
     dot.setAttribute('stroke', '#8a6d1a');
     board.append(dot);
   }
   ```

Five yellow circles in a row, each one touching the next. `STEP` is the
distance between two centers, and `col * STEP` turns the loop counter into a
position. Now wrap a loop over rows around the loop over columns, and let the
row decide `cy`:

```ts
for (let row = 0; row < 5; row++) {
  for (let col = 0; col < 5; col++) {
    const dot = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
    dot.setAttribute('cx', String(26 + col * STEP));
    dot.setAttribute('cy', String(26 + row * STEP));
    dot.setAttribute('r', '26');
    dot.setAttribute('fill', '#f7d774');
    dot.setAttribute('stroke', '#8a6d1a');
    board.append(dot);
  }
}
```

Twenty-five circles in a square grid, with a hole between every four of them.

## The half step that closes the holes {#sec-beehive-offset}

Push every second row half a step to the right, and pull the rows closer
together. Add these above the loops:

```ts
const ROW_STEP = 45;

const rowOffset = (row: number) => {
  if (row % 2 === 1) {
    return STEP / 2;
  }

  return 0;
};
```

Then change the two position lines inside the inner loop:

```ts
dot.setAttribute('cx', String(26 + col * STEP + rowOffset(row)));
dot.setAttribute('cy', String(26 + row * ROW_STEP));
```

Reload, and the holes are gone. `row % 2 === 1` picks rows 1 and 3, so the
second and the fourth row move half a step sideways, and the smaller `ROW_STEP`
lets each row drop into the dents of the row above it. The whole layout now sits
in `STEP`, `ROW_STEP`, and the two loop bounds, so a bigger board is a change to
four numbers and to nothing in the drawing code.

## One shape, placed 25 times {#sec-beehive-use}

Circles leave thin gaps along their sides. Hexagons do not, which is why a real
comb is built from them, and a hexagon in SVG is a `<polygon>` with six points.
Writing those points 25 times would mean 25 polygons carrying 300 numbers
between them, all describing one shape in different places. SVG has a way out:
keep one copy of the shape and stamp it onto the picture as often as you like,
each stamp with its own `x` and `y`, which is exactly what your two loops
compute. The element names are `<defs>`, `<symbol>`, and `<use>`; the research
box below sends you to MDN for how they fit together.

## State first, picture second {#sec-beehive-state}

The bee in the exercise stands on one cell. Where does that fact live? You could
read the bee's `x` attribute back out of the document, add a step, and write it
back. Or you keep a variable of your own:

```ts
const beePosition = { col: 0, row: 0 };
```

Take the variable. An attribute hands you a string in pixels, while every rule
of the game is about columns and rows. "Stay inside the hive" is
`col >= 0 && col < 5` on two small integers. In pixels, with the offset of every
second row mixed in, the same rule turns into arithmetic nobody wants to debug.

So the object holds what is true, and the picture only shows it. A move changes
the object and then redraws:

```ts
const moveBee = (deltaCol: number, deltaRow: number) => {
  beePosition.col += deltaCol;
  beePosition.row += deltaRow;
  drawBee();
};
```

`drawBee` computes the pixel center of `beePosition`'s cell and writes it into
the bee element. The guard that keeps the bee inside the hive belongs at the top
of `moveBee`, and the exercise asks you for it.

## Two ways to ask for the same move {#sec-beehive-controls}

Because `moveBee` exists, wiring a button to it takes one line:

```ts
rightButton.addEventListener('click', () => moveBee(1, 0));
```

The keyboard needs a single listener, and it goes on `document`. A `keydown`
listener on a button only fires while that button has the focus, and nobody
wants to click the page before they may play.

`event.key` says which key went down. You read it for letters in Part 2; the
arrow keys carry names of their own, and the research box asks you for all four.
A `switch (event.key)` with one `case` per arrow reads better than four `if`s,
and a `default` that returns leaves every other key alone. Arrow keys also do
something of their own in a browser, and `event.preventDefault()` is the line
that stops it. What exactly it stops is the last research question.

Both paths end in the same `moveBee`, so a rule you add later lives in one
place. And the buttons are what make the game playable on a phone.

## The pad is a three by three grid {#sec-beehive-pad}

Four arrows around a honey button, and CSS Grid places them without a single
wrapper `div`:

```css
#pad {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 3rem);
  grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 3rem);
}

#up {
  grid-column: 2;
  grid-row: 1;
}
```

Each button names its own column and row, so the order in the HTML does not
decide where it lands. The stylesheet for the exercise carries all five
placements.

::: {.research title="Six corners, one symbol, and the arrow keys"}
The hive you are about to build is one hexagon defined once and placed 25 times,
and the bee walks through it with the arrow keys. You have seen neither of those
in this book.

1. A regular hexagon has six corners, all at the same distance from its center.
   Given the center point and that distance, how do you compute the six corner
   points with `Math.cos` and `Math.sin`? And which unit do those two functions
   want the angle in?
2. What are `<defs>`, `<symbol>`, and `<use>` for in an SVG, and which attribute
   of `<use>` names the symbol it places?
3. A `keydown` handler reads `event.key`. What are the four values you get for
   the four arrow keys?
4. What does `event.preventDefault()` stop when you call it inside a `keydown`
   handler?

Questions 1 and 3 are exam material: you write this kind of code with no
internet and no AI next to you.
:::

## Exercise: the beehive {#sec-beehive-exercise}

A hive of 25 cells, and a bee that leaves a honey pot wherever you send it.

{{< exercise beehive >}}

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/` (or `homework/`).
   Read
   `index.html`: an `<svg id="hive">` with an empty `<symbol id="hex">` inside
   `<defs>`, two empty groups `#cells` and `#pots`, a `<text id="bee">`, a
   status paragraph, and five buttons inside `#pad`. Run `npm start`. Expected
   result: pad and status line show up, the hive area is empty, and half a bee
   sticks out of the top left corner.
2. In `src/index.ts`, write `import './styles.css';`, the namespace constant
   `const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';`, and the layout constants:

   ```ts
   const COLUMNS = 5;
   const ROWS = 5;
   const RADIUS = 30;
   const STEP_X = Math.sqrt(3) * RADIUS;
   const STEP_Y = 1.5 * RADIUS;
   ```

   `RADIUS` is the distance from a cell's center to one of its corners,
   `STEP_X` the horizontal distance between two centers in one row, `STEP_Y` the
   distance between two rows. The last two follow from the hexagon's shape; take
   them as given.
3. Look up the elements with `querySelector<...>` and cover them with one `if`
   that throws: `#hex` (`SVGSymbolElement`), `#cells` and `#pots`
   (`SVGGElement`), `#bee` (`SVGTextElement`), `#status`
   (`HTMLParagraphElement`), and the buttons `#up`, `#down`, `#left`, `#right`,
   `#drop` (`HTMLButtonElement`). Write every helper below as
   `const drawBee = () => { ... };` so the null check keeps holding inside it.
4. Add the position helpers. The box around the cell in column `col` and row
   `row` has its top left corner here:

   ```ts
   const rowOffset = (row: number) => {
     if (row % 2 === 1) {
       return STEP_X / 2;
     }

     return 0;
   };

   const cellLeft = (col: number, row: number) => col * STEP_X + rowOffset(row);
   const cellTop = (row: number) => row * STEP_Y;
   ```

   The center of that cell is `cellLeft(col, row) + STEP_X / 2` across and
   `cellTop(row) + RADIUS` down. Cells are placed by the corner, the bee by the
   center.
5. Fill the symbol. Write a helper that creates one `<polygon>`, sets its
   `points` attribute to the six corners of a hexagon, and appends it to `#hex`.
   Put that hexagon's center at `STEP_X / 2` across and `RADIUS` down, never at
   `(0, 0)`: a symbol draws nothing above or to the left of its own origin, so
   negative corners vanish. Build the attribute in a loop that runs six times,
   pushing strings such as `'25.98,0'` into an array and joining them with a
   space. Expected result: the page still shows no hive, and your answer to
   research question 2 says why.
6. Place the cells. Write a helper that takes a group, a class name, a column,
   and a row, creates a `<use>` element pointing at the hexagon symbol, sets its
   `x` and `y` from `cellLeft` and `cellTop`, adds the class, and appends it to
   the group. Call it from a nested loop over `ROWS` and `COLUMNS` with the
   class `cell` and the group `#cells`. Expected result: 25 golden hexagons in
   five offset rows with no gaps, and a cell that brightens under the mouse.
7. Give the bee a home. Add `const beePosition = { col: 0, row: 0 };` and
   `let potCount = 0;`. Write `drawBee`, which sets the `x` and `y` attributes
   of the bee element to the center of `beePosition`'s cell, and `showStatus`,
   which puts a line such as `Bee at column 0, row 0. 0 honey pots.` into the
   status paragraph. Call both once after the cells are placed. Expected result:
   the bee sits in the middle of the top left cell.
8. Make it move. Write `moveBee(deltaCol, deltaRow)`: compute the new column and
   row, `return` without changing anything when either one falls outside 0 to 4,
   otherwise store them and call `drawBee` and `showStatus`. Wire the four arrow
   buttons with one `click` listener each: up is `(0, -1)`, down `(0, 1)`, left
   `(-1, 0)`, right `(1, 0)`. Expected result: the bee walks and stops at the
   border. It zig-zags going up and down, which is right, because the cell above
   cell `(2, 3)` does sit half a step to the left.
9. Drop honey. Write `dropHoney`, which places a hexagon with the class `honey`
   in the `#pots` group at the bee's cell, counts the pot, and refreshes the
   status line. That is the helper from step 6 again with two other arguments.
   Wire it to `#drop`. Expected result: the cell under the bee turns orange, the
   counter grows, and the bee stays visible on top of the pot.
10. Add the keyboard. Listen for `keydown` on `document`, `switch` on
    `event.key`, call `moveBee` in one `case` per arrow key, and end the switch
    with `default: return;`. Call `event.preventDefault()` after the switch.
    Expected result: the arrow keys move the bee. Make the window short enough
    to scroll, comment the `preventDefault` line out, and press an arrow key to
    see what that line does for you.
11. Bonus: refuse a second pot on a cell that already holds one. Keep the pots
    in an array of `{ col: number; row: number }` objects and search it in
    `dropHoney`. Second bonus: let the space bar drop honey too.
12. Run `npm run check` and `npx tsc --noEmit`, and fix what they report.

::: {.callout-note}
## What has to work

* The app starts with `npm start`, the console stays free of errors, and
  `npm run check` and `npx tsc --noEmit` pass.
* The hive shows 25 hexagons in five offset rows, with no gaps between them.
* The five buttons sit in a pad, with the four arrows around the honey button.
* The bee moves left and right with the buttons and never leaves the hive.
* The honey button leaves a pot on the cell the bee stands on.

Movement up and down, and the arrow keys, are what lift this above passing.
:::

Keep the project. The next chapter looks at the project itself: where images
and `.svg` files live, and what `npm run build` writes into `dist/`.
